title: Article analysis: screen time and attention in teenagers

readings.title: Is recreational screen time related to attention in teenagers?
readings.html:
Introduction

Many parents worry that time on phones and other screens harms teenagers’ attention. The researchers asked whether daily recreational screen time is related to performance on an attention task.

Participants

Twenty students (ages 13 to 15; 11 girls and 9 boys) from two junior high schools (grades 7 to 9) in one suburban school district in Canada took part. Parents signed consent forms and each student agreed to take part after the study was explained. Students were told they could stop at any time. Each student’s results were stored under a code number rather than a name.

Method

For one week, each student’s phone and computer recorded their recreational screen time (games, video and social media, not schoolwork); the researchers used each student’s average hours per day. At the end of the week, each student completed a 10-minute computer attention task: letters flashed on the screen one at a time, and the student pressed a key only when an X appeared. Attention was the number of the 30 X’s that the student correctly responded to.

Results

Students with more daily screen time tended to respond correctly to fewer X’s (r=−.52r = -.52; see the scatterplot).

Discussion

The researchers noted that they did not measure sleep, family rules about screens or students’ interest in the task. Larger real studies of teenagers usually find weaker relationships between screen time and attention than this one.

Invented study for practice.

parts.label: A
parts.prompt: Identify the research method used in the study.

rubric.point: Identifies the method as a correlational study.

parts.sample: The study is a correlational study: the researchers measured screen time and attention as they occurred and did not assign students to amounts of screen time.

parts.label: B
parts.prompt: State the operational definition of attention in the study.

rubric.point: States attention as the number of the 30 X’s a student correctly responded to (by pressing the key) on the 10-minute computer task.
accept: how many of the 30 X’s each student correctly pressed the key for in the 10-minute task
the number of correct key presses to the 30 X’s

parts.sample: Attention was the number of the 30 X’s that a student correctly pressed the key for during the 10-minute computer task.

parts.label: C
parts.prompt: Describe what the correlation coefficient shows about the relationship between screen time and attention in this study.

rubric.point: Describes a moderate negative correlation: students with more daily screen time tended to respond correctly to fewer X’s (r = -.52).
accept: a negative correlation: as screen time went up, correct responses tended to go down
students who used screens more tended to score lower on the attention task, a moderate relationship

parts.sample: The correlation of -.52 is moderate and negative: students who spent more hours a day on recreational screens tended to respond correctly to fewer of the 30 X’s, although the points are fairly scattered, so the relationship is far from perfect.

parts.label: D
parts.prompt: Identify one ethical guideline the researchers followed and describe how they applied it in this study.

rubric.point: Identifies a guideline described in the summary (parental consent with student assent, right to withdraw, confidentiality) and describes how it was applied.
accept: informed assent: parents signed consent forms and each student agreed after the study was explained
confidentiality: each student’s results were stored under a code number rather than a name
right to withdraw: students were told they could stop at any time

parts.sample: The researchers protected confidentiality: each student’s screen time and attention scores were stored under a code number instead of the student’s name, so no result could be traced to a particular student.

parts.label: E
parts.prompt: Explain the extent to which the results can be generalized to teenagers in the United States.

rubric.point: Explains the extent of generalizability using characteristics of the participants (20 students aged 13 to 15 from two suburban junior high schools in one Canadian district) compared with U.S. teenagers.
accept: only partly: the participants were young teens like many U.S. teenagers, but all came from two suburban junior high schools in one Canadian district and none were older teens
limited, because the participants were 13 to 15 years old from one suburban district in Canada, not teenagers of all ages from cities, towns and rural areas

parts.sample: Only partly. The participants were 13- to 15-year-olds, so they resemble younger U.S. teenagers, and Canadian suburban students may use screens in similar ways. But all came from two junior high schools in one suburban district in Canada and none were 16 to 19, so the results may not describe older teenagers or those in cities or rural areas.

parts.label: F
parts.prompt: Explain why the results do not show that screen time causes poorer attention.

rubric.point: Uses a specific, accurate result: students with more screen time responded correctly to fewer X’s (a negative correlation).
accept: the correlation of -.52 between screen time and correct responses
students who used screens more tended to have lower attention scores

rubric.point: Explains that the study is correlational, so a third variable (such as sleep, which the researchers did not measure) or the reverse direction (students who already have trouble focusing may choose more screen time) could explain the relationship.
accept: less sleep could both raise screen time and lower attention, and sleep was not measured
students who find it hard to focus may turn to screens more, so attention could affect screen time rather than the reverse

parts.sample: The results do not show cause. Students with more screen time did tend to score lower on the attention task (r = -.52), but the researchers only measured both variables; they did not assign anyone to screen time. A third variable they did not measure, such as sleep, could explain the pattern: students who stay up late may use screens more and also be less alert during the task. The direction could also run the other way, since students who already have trouble focusing may turn to games and video more often.
